w: Money, time and interest Why a euro today and a euro in ten years' time are different quantities, what interest is made up of, and where the line runs between saving, investing and speculating. A twenty-euro note is printed cotton paper with a security thread. Its value rests on the expectation that others will continue to accept it in future as payment for work, goods or services. Money is therefore a **claim on future goods**. How much you get for it depends on prices at the time of purchase, and those prices change. A sum of money therefore always comes with a point in time. €1,000 today and €1,000 in ten years cannot be compared directly, in the same way that 100 kilometres and 100 kilometres per hour are different quantities. A comparison that ignores the point in time leads to wrong decisions, and does so systematically in favour of the distant payment, whose amount looks larger than its value today would justify. Money is a claim on future goods. Its value depends on what you get for it and at what point in time, and not on the nominal amount alone. ## The components of interest Anyone who lends or invests money gives up something certain, namely immediate command over purchasing power. w: Compound interest Why a constant interest rate has an uneven effect, and why the term sits in the exponent of the compound interest formula. Interest and compound interest differ only in what happens to the interest credited. If €100 is invested at 5% and the interest is withdrawn every year, the amount credited is always €5, for all fifty years. If the interest stays in the account instead, the credit is €5.25 in the second year, €7.76 in the tenth, €20.58 in the thirtieth and €54.61 in the fiftieth. In the fiftieth year alone, more than half of the capital originally invested is added. The bank pays only the agreed interest throughout. The interest rate stays at 5% the whole time; what grows is the base to which it is applied. With [[Compound interest|compound interest]], the interest is therefore not paid out, it is added to the capital and earns interest itself the following year. The two calculations differ in the way repeated addition differs from repeated multiplication. With linear growth, the same amount is added in each period; with exponential growth, the total is multiplied by the same factor in each period. At first the difference is small. w: Risk and volatility Why the financial industry measures risk as fluctuation, while investors usually take it to mean a loss, and which risks the volatility figure does not capture. The other asks whether the money will still be there in twelve years' time, when the property has to be paid for. Both questions are legitimate, but only the first can be expressed precisely in a single number. That is why this number appears in every prospectus. s: Why a loss and a gain of the same size do not cancel each other out, and what this asymmetry means for volatility and leverage.
w: The arithmetic of losses Why a loss and a gain of the same size do not cancel each other out, and what this asymmetry means for volatility and leverage. A portfolio loses 30% in one year and gains 30% the next. The average of the two years is zero, yet afterwards the portfolio stands at 91% of its starting value. This is because the two percentages refer to different amounts. The loss is deducted from the full capital, while the gain is added to the reduced remainder. After minus 30%, €10,000 becomes €7,000. For this to become €10,000 again, €3,000 has to be earned on a base of €7,000, which is 42.9%. With small losses, this gap between the loss and the necessary recovery is small; with large losses, it grows sharply. The loss is measured against the original capital, the recovery against the smaller remainder. Equal percentages for loss and gain therefore do not offset each other. Mathematically, every percentage point of loss avoided is worth more than an additional percentage point of gain. ## Average return and final wealth This asymmetry does not only take effect after a crash. It is present in every series of returns, including a predominantly positive one. Two portfolios with the same annual average reach different final values as soon as one of them fluctuates, and the fluctuating portfolio always comes off worse. Both portfolios start with €10,000 and run for 20 years.

w: The order of steps in building wealth Why choosing an ETF only comes sixth, and which steps should be completed before it. w: Essential and dispensable insurance Which risks justify insurance, which four policies cover the risks that threaten your livelihood, and which policies you can do without. The price of this promise is made up of the expected loss plus loadings for administration, distribution and profit margin. Across the insured pool as a whole, policyholders therefore inevitably pay in more than they get out, because otherwise no insurer could survive. This gives rise to the most important rule when choosing insurance. Losses that can be paid from the emergency fund or from two months' salary are ones you bear yourself. The reason is that the loading for administration and distribution is highest in percentage terms for small losses. w: Gross, net and the marginal tax rate How income tax and social security contributions, two deduction systems with opposite logic, lead from gross to net pay, and why the marginal tax rate is decisive for almost every financial decision. The higher the taxable income, the larger the share that goes in tax. Social security contributions, by contrast, are levied at a fixed percentage, but only up to a ceiling. No contributions are due on income above it. s: Why every purchase has three prices, only the first of which is on the label, and what this means for cars, subscriptions and pay rises.
w: The cost of consumption Why every purchase has three prices, only the first of which is on the label, and what this means for cars, subscriptions and pay rises. Every purchase has three prices. The first is the purchase price on the label. The second is incurred continuously for as long as the thing exists, for example for insurance, electricity, maintenance, fees and parking. The third, which is never stated anywhere, is the return that the tied-up money would have earned over the same period if it had been used differently. A comparison that considers only the first price therefore rests on a third of the information. Distinguishing between the three prices has nothing to do with morality. A car that costs three hundred euros a month in depreciation is justifiable if it is worth three hundred euros a month to its owner. It only becomes a mistake if nobody ever worked out that it is three hundred euros a month. ## Lifestyle inflation The term [[lifestyle inflation]] is used when spending rises with income rather than with prices. w: Creditworthiness, SCHUFA and keeping your finances in order How contracts and payment behaviour turn into a score, what a weak score costs in interest, and which precautions keep your finances working even in an emergency. Every contract in which one side performs first is a form of credit. Examples are the flat before the first rent payment, the mobile phone contract with a subsidised handset, buying on invoice, leasing and the instalment loan. The side that performs first wants to know how likely it is to get its money back. To find out, it asks a credit reference agency, not the person concerned. [[Creditworthiness]] is therefore not a judgement of character. It determines the terms you are offered, even though you usually do not know your own score. ## What a credit reference agency holds A credit reference agency collects data on contract and payment behaviour. This includes which accounts, cards, loans, leases and mobile phone contracts exist and how long they have been running, whether instalments are paid on time, and whether there are reminder procedures, debt collection, court orders or insolvency entries. Income, wealth, occupation, nationality and religious affiliation are not stored. A poor score is therefore almost always the result of contracts and late payments, not of poverty. w: Partnership, children and inheritance How couples split shared costs, who owns a child's securities account and how much tax is due on inheritances and gifts. What needs to be settled is who bears which share of the shared costs, who owns the wealth built up for children, and who decides and inherits if something happens to one of the partners. These are tailored to a model that many households no longer live: a married couple with one main earner and children together. s: Which three functions money performs, how cash and account balances differ as two kinds of euro, and why today's money is backed by trust alone.
w: What money is Which three functions money performs, how cash and account balances differ as two kinds of euro, and why today's money is backed by trust alone. What money is follows from the functions it performs. A ten-euro note is printed cotton fibre, a balance in a current account is a line in a bank's database, a gold coin is a piece of metal. None of these objects is money in itself. They count as money only as long as other people accept them in exchange. The material therefore does not tell you whether something is money. What matters is what an object has to do in order to serve as money. ## The three functions of money As a **medium of exchange**, money removes the need for the double coincidence of wants that all trade without money requires. In direct barter, the baker has to need shoes, and at exactly the moment when the shoemaker wants bread. Money splits this unlikely exchange into two transactions, each of which is easy to arrange. This makes money convenient, and it also determines how far the division of labour can develop. As a **unit of account**, money provides the yardstick in which all prices are expressed. Without this yardstick, every good would have to be valued against every other good. s: Most money is created as a book entry at a commercial bank when it grants a loan, and not in the printing press.
w: How money is created Most money is created as a book entry at a commercial bank when it grants a loan, and not in the printing press. A bank grants a loan of €300,000. The transaction can be shown in two lines of bookkeeping. On the assets side, a claim on the borrower is created; on the liabilities side, a sight deposit of the same amount is created and credited to her current account. No other account is debited, and no saver loses anything. The bank's balance sheet is then €300,000 larger than before, and the economy's money supply has grown by the same amount. This contradicts the widespread idea that a bank collects savings deposits and passes them on as loans. The Deutsche Bundesbank explicitly rejected this idea in its Monthly Report of April 2017. The report states that a bank can grant loans without any prior inflows of customer deposits The deposit is therefore the result of lending and not its precondition. The process also works in reverse. If the borrower repays €1,000, the claim on the assets side falls by this amount, and €1,000 of book money disappears on the liabilities side. The money used for the repayment thereby ceases to exist. An economy's money supply therefore only grows as long as more new loans are granted than are repaid. ## Two separate money circuits Two different kinds of money circulate side by side in the monetary system. s: A central bank directly sets only a single price and depends on banks and markets to pass it on to the rest of the economy.
w: Goals and instruments of central banks A central bank directly sets only a single price and depends on banks and markets to pass it on to the rest of the economy. A central bank produces nothing and sells nothing, and measured against its impact it has only a few employees. It directly determines only a single price, the overnight interest rate for central bank money. w: The euro crisis and negative interest rates How a banking crisis became a sovereign debt crisis, what Draghi's pledge in July 2012 achieved and how eight years of negative interest rates affected German savings. In October 2009, the new Greek government revised the budget deficit for the current year from 3.7% to 12.7% of economic output. The debt ratio had risen from 104.6% to 128.5% between 2007 and 2009. Within months, the statistical correction turned into the question of whether the single currency would survive. A state with its own central bank can erode the value of its debts through inflation or devalue its currency. A member of a monetary union cannot do this. It is left with three options: cutting spending, accepting help or stopping payments. During the euro crisis, the choice between these options was fought over for six years. ## From bank debt to government debt The euro crisis was the continuation of the 2008 financial crisis. When governments supported their banks, the banks' losses passed into public budgets. The debt ratio of today's 27 EU member states jumped from 65.1% of GDP (2008) to 75.7% (2009). This was most evident in Ireland. The Irish state guaranteed the liabilities of its banks in 2008, and the deficit reached over 30% of economic output in 2010. w: Expected value, Kelly and the probability of ruin Why the same strategy multiplies or destroys capital depending on position size, and where the limit lies mathematically. Two traders trade the same signal. Both are right in 40% of cases and have a reward-to-risk ratio (RRR) of 1.8, so the expected value per trade is positive for both. One risks 1% of capital per position, the other 20%. After 1,000 trades, the first has tripled their money, while the second has around one fifty-thousandth of their starting capital left. The difference is due neither to discipline nor to bad luck; it follows from the arithmetic. The expected value per trade is an **arithmetic mean**. It describes what comes out on average across many traders trading in parallel.
